In September 2013, [Jiang Jiemin](/wiki/Jiang_Jiemin "Jiang Jiemin"), a former chairman of PetroChina, was abruptly removed from his role as director of the [State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council](/wiki/State-owned_Assets_Supervision_and_Administration_Commission_of_the_State_Council "State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission of the State Council") and investigated for corruption and abuse of power, along with four other senior oil executives.[[52]](#cite_note-52) [Jiang](/wiki/Jiang_Jiemin "Jiang Jiemin") was considered an ally of corrupt former security chief [Zhou Yongkang](/wiki/Zhou_Yongkang "Zhou Yongkang"), and part of a group of officials that had political ties with Zhou. On 12 October 2015, the court found [Jiang](/wiki/Jiang_Jiemin "Jiang Jiemin") guilty on all counts, including accepting bribes, possessing dark assets, and abusing his power. He was sentenced to 16 years in prison.[[53]](#cite_note-53)

In January 2017, former vice chairman [Liao Yongyuan](/wiki/Liao_Yongyuan "Liao Yongyuan") was sentenced to 15 years in prison for abuse of power and accepting nearly $2 million worth of bribes.[[54]](#cite_note-54)[[55]](#cite_note-55)

In October 2021, the [Central Commission for Discipline Inspection](/wiki/Central_Commission_for_Discipline_Inspection "Central Commission for Discipline Inspection") announced that it was investigating former vice president Ling Xiao, for "serious disciplinary violations".[[56]](#cite_note-56)

In January 2014, the [International Consortium of Investigative Journalists](/wiki/International_Consortium_of_Investigative_Journalists "International Consortium of Investigative Journalists") published research based on leaked financial records from the [British Virgin Islands](/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands "British Virgin Islands"), implicating [CNPC](/wiki/China_National_Petroleum_Corporation "China National Petroleum Corporation"), PetroChina, [Sinopec](/wiki/Sinopec "Sinopec"), and [CNOOC](/wiki/China_National_Offshore_Oil_Corporation "China National Offshore Oil Corporation") in offshore tax evasion.[[57]

Despite the inherent difficulties in accounting for inflation, several attempts have been made. Estimates depend on the [price index](/wiki/Price_index "Price index") used to adjust the grosses,[[31]](#cite_note-Leonhardt-116) and the [exchange rates](/wiki/Exchange_rate "Exchange rate") used to convert between currencies can also affect the calculations, both of which can have an effect on the ultimate rankings of an inflation adjusted list. *Gone with the Wind*—first released in 1939—is generally considered to be the most successful film, with *[Guinness World Records](/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records")* in 2014 estimating its adjusted global gross at $3.4 billion. Estimates for *Gone with the Wind*'s adjusted gross have varied substantially: its owner, [Turner Entertainment](/wiki/Turner_Entertainment "Turner Entertainment"), estimated its adjusted earnings at $3.3 billion in 2007, a few years earlier than the *Guinness* estimate;[[32]](#cite_note-gwtw_tcm-117) other estimates fall either side of this amount, with one putting its gross just under $3 billion in 2010,[[33]](#cite_note-Shone-118) while another provided an alternative figure of $3.8 billion in 2006.[[34]](#cite_note-119) Which film is *Gone with the Wind*'s nearest rival depends on the set of figures used: *Guinness* had *Avatar* in second place with $3 billion, while other estimates saw *Titanic* in the runner-up spot with first-run worldwide earnings of almost $2.9 billion at 2010 prices.[[33]](#cite_note-Shone-118)

By convention, continents "are understood to be large, continuous, discrete masses of land, ideally separated by expanses of water".[[9]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis_&_Wigen,_The_Myth_of_Continents199721-9) By this definition, all continents have to be an island of some metric. In modern schemes with five or more recognized continents, at least one pair of continents is joined by land in some fashion. The criterion "large" leads to arbitrary classification: [Greenland](/wiki/Greenland "Greenland"), with a surface area of 2,166,086 square kilometres (836,330 sq mi), is only considered the world's largest island, while [Australia](/wiki/Australia_(continent) "Australia (continent)"), at 7,617,930 square kilometres (2,941,300 sq mi), is deemed the smallest continent.

Earth's major landmasses all have coasts on a single, continuous [World Ocean](/wiki/Ocean#World_Ocean "Ocean"), which is divided into several principal oceanic components by the continents and various geographic criteria.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-UNAoO-11)

The geological definition of a continent has four criteria: high elevation relative to the ocean floor; a wide range of igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks rich in silica; a crust thicker than the surrounding oceanic crust; and well-defined limits around a large enough area.[[12]](#cite_note-nytimes.com-12)

The President's House (1862–1897) at Columbia's Midtown campus

At Columbia's midtown Manhattan campus (1857–1896), a house for the president was built in 1862 near the corner of 49th Street and [Fourth Avenue](/wiki/Park_Avenue "Park Avenue") (later Park Avenue), which served as the home of both Charles King and Frederick Augustus Porter Barnard. It was the president's official residence until that campus' demolition in 1897.

The current house for the president of Columbia University, located on the university's [Morningside Heights](/wiki/Morningside_Heights "Morningside Heights") campus, was built in 1912, and has served as the official residence of the university president since, with the exception of during the tenure of Michael Sovern, who chose to instead continue living in his Upper East Side apartment. The house was reoccupied upon the accession of George Rupp in 1993, and has remained in use since then.[[54]](#cite_note-78)

Demolition of the building was considered as late as 1991,[[55]](#cite_note-79) though the building underwent a comprehensive renovation in 2005.[[56]](#cite_note-80)
